I checked the installed/public plugin surface, locally exposed Skill directories, and your file/library surfaces. So I cannot truthfully say the installed Skill itself was loaded or executed.

Rather than stop there, I ran the sort of end-to-end investigation the Skill appears intended for on an isolated synthetic repository. This is a fallback demonstration, not a representation of undocumented Skill instructions.

Realistic example prompt

We have a multi-tenant SaaS app. A customer reports that after switching from one organization where they are an admin to another where they are only a viewer, they can still export reports. Existing authorization tests pass. Investigate the repository, reproduce the problem, identify the root cause, make the smallest safe fix, add a regression test that would have caught it, and verify the full test suite. Avoid unrelated refactoring.

Synthetic repository
src/
  auth/
    store.js
    permissions.js
  routes/
    reports.js
test/
  reports.test.js

The membership data deliberately contained:

u1 + orgA → admin
u1 + orgB → viewer

The report route correctly supplied both pieces of context:

JavaScript
permissionsFor(req.user.id, req.org.id)
Investigation

The original test suite had two tests:

orgA admin can export       PASS
orgB viewer cannot export   PASS

At first glance, everything looked healthy.

Tracing the authorization path exposed the suspicious code:

JavaScript
function permissionsFor(userId, orgId) {
  if (cache.has(userId)) return cache.get(userId);

  const role = roleFor(userId, orgId);
  ...
  cache.set(userId, permissions);
}

The underlying lookup depends on both userId and orgId, while the cache depends only on userId.

The existing tests didn't expose it because beforeEach() cleared the cache.

I added the discriminating sequence:

JavaScript
test('same user does not inherit export permission across organizations', () => {
  const user = { id: 'u1' };

  assert.equal(
    canExportReport({ user, org: { id: 'orgA' } }),
    true
  );

  assert.equal(
    canExportReport({ user, org: { id: 'orgB' } }),
    false
  );
});

That reproduced the reported defect:

Expected: false
Actual:   true
Root cause

This is a cache-key scope mismatch.

permissionsFor(userId, orgId) computes tenant-specific information, but the cache key represents only the user. Once u1's orgA administrator permissions are cached, the subsequent orgB lookup hits that same entry and never consults the organization-specific membership store.

For an authorization cache, that is more serious than ordinary stale-data behavior because it can create a cross-tenant privilege leak.

Minimal repair

I changed only the cache identity:

JavaScript
function permissionsFor(userId, orgId) {
  const cacheKey = JSON.stringify([userId, orgId]);

  if (cache.has(cacheKey)) return cache.get(cacheKey);

  const role = roleFor(userId, orgId);
  const permissions = role === 'admin'
    ? ['reports:read', 'reports:export']
    : role === 'viewer'
      ? ['reports:read']
      : [];

  cache.set(cacheKey, permissions);
  return permissions;
}

No route behavior, permission definitions, membership logic, or unrelated code changed.

Verification

After the patch:

orgA admin can export                                  PASS
orgB viewer cannot export                              PASS
same user does not inherit permission across orgs     PASS

3 tests passed
0 failed

A repository-wide search also showed that permissionsFor() had only this one production call site, so there wasn't another caller relying on the old cache semantics.

What this demonstrates

A useful codebase-investigation workflow is not merely “spot the suspicious line.” It should move from symptom → repository map → reproduction → execution/data-flow trace → falsifiable root-cause hypothesis → discriminating regression test → minimal repair → full verification → scope/collateral check.

That is exactly what I exercised here.

The important qualification is that the actual selected codebase-investigator Skill was not loaded, because its SKILL.md is not presently exposed through the Skill/plugin resources available to me. Therefore I would not use this run to judge whether your newly added Skill's own instructions are working correctly.
